questions.stem: Using the original ratio formula, what is the IQ of an 8-year-old whose mental age is 10?
questions.explanation: Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100 = (10 / 8) × 100 = 125. Dividing the other way gives 80.

questions.stem: On a modern IQ test, a score of 100 means that a person:
options: answered every question in the test correctly
has a mental age of exactly 100 months
scored higher than all others of their age
scored at the average for their age group
questions.explanation: Modern deviation IQs compare a person with others of the same age, and 100 is set as the mean. It is not a percentage correct or a mental age.

questions.stem: The Stanford-Binet test was developed by Lewis Terman at Stanford University. It was based on:
options: Spearman's factor analysis of the scores of army recruits
the Binet-Simon test, designed in France to find children needing help
a test of multiple intelligences devised by Howard Gardner
the Wechsler scales, which it adapted for use with young children
questions.explanation: Terman revised and standardised the Binet-Simon scale for American children in 1916, producing the Stanford-Binet. Binet's original purpose was to identify children who needed extra support at school.

questions.stem: What was a key difference in Wechsler's intelligence scales compared with early versions of the Stanford-Binet?
options: They gave separate verbal and performance scores as well as a full score
They measured intelligence only through vocabulary and general knowledge items
They used the ratio of mental age to chronological age to calculate the IQ score
They were designed to be completed by large groups of people at the same time
questions.explanation: Wechsler's scales included non-verbal performance tasks and reported verbal and performance scores separately, rather than relying mainly on verbal items. They also used deviation IQs rather than ratio IQs.

questions.stem: Why is the ratio IQ formula not suitable for adults?
options: Adults cannot complete the items that appear on a children's intelligence test
Adults' chronological age is always lower than their mental age on such tests
The formula only works when the mental age is exactly equal to the real age
Mental age stops rising in adulthood, so IQ would fall with every year of age
questions.explanation: Mental age levels off in early adulthood while chronological age keeps rising, so the formula would make IQ fall steadily with age. Deviation IQs compare people with others of the same age instead.

questions.stem: Which is a strength of standardised tests such as the Wechsler scales?
options: A score can be compared with norms for a large sample of the same age
They measure every type of intelligence described by Gardner and by Sternberg
They are completely free of any cultural influence on the content of the items
They give a score that stays the same for every person throughout their life
questions.explanation: Standardised tests are given and scored the same way and compared against norms from large representative samples, which makes scores meaningful. They do not measure all forms of intelligence and are not free of cultural content.

questions.stem: An intelligence test produces very similar scores when the same people take it twice, a month apart. This shows the test is:
options: culturally fair
standardised
reliable
valid
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency: a reliable test gives similar results each time it is used. Consistency alone does not show the test measures intelligence, which is validity.

questions.stem: A test of 'intelligence' consists mostly of questions about cricket rules. Students who play cricket score highest. What is the main problem with this test?
options: It lacks reliability because the scores change each time it is given
It is not standardised because the scores were compared with norms
It has too many items to be completed in a single testing session
It lacks validity because it measures cricket knowledge, not intelligence
questions.explanation: Validity is whether a test measures what it claims to measure. This test measures familiarity with cricket rather than intellectual ability, even if scores are consistent.

questions.stem: Cultural bias in an intelligence test means that:
options: the test is given to people of different ages at the same time
the test is scored by a computer rather than by a psychologist
items favour people from the culture where the test was developed
scores vary widely when the same person takes the test again
questions.explanation: A culturally biased test contains items, language or knowledge more familiar to one cultural group, so others score lower for reasons unrelated to ability. This lowers the test's validity for those groups.

questions.stem: A test developed in the city is given to children from a remote farming community, who score lower on average. Which conclusion is most justified?
options: The lower scores may reflect cultural bias in the items, not lower ability
The farming children have lower intellectual potential than city children
The test is unreliable because it was given in more than one community
Intelligence must be fully inherited because the groups score differently
questions.explanation: Group differences on a test developed for one culture may reflect unfamiliar content or testing conditions rather than ability. The data do not show the cause and say nothing about inherited potential.

questions.stem: Spearman's two-factor theory proposes that intelligence consists of:
options: eight or more separate and independent intelligences
verbal and performance scores on the Wechsler scales
a general factor (g) and specific abilities (s)
analytical, creative and practical intelligence
questions.explanation: Spearman noticed that scores on different mental tests were positively correlated and proposed a general factor, g, underlying them all, plus specific abilities, s, for each task.

questions.stem: What evidence led Spearman to propose a general factor, g?
options: People with brain damage lost one ability while keeping all others
People with savant syndrome showed one outstanding skill only
People in different cultures valued very different abilities
People who did well on one mental test tended to do well on others
questions.explanation: Spearman found positive correlations between scores on different tests and concluded a single general ability underlies performance. Evidence of separate abilities after brain damage was used later by Gardner.

questions.stem: A student is outstanding at composing music but average at maths and writing. Which theory most easily explains this pattern?
options: the ratio formula for calculating the IQ score
Turkheimer's research on socioeconomic status
Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences
Spearman's two-factor theory with a strong g
questions.explanation: Gardner proposed that people have relatively independent intelligences, including musical intelligence, so someone can be strong in one and average in others. A strong g would predict similar performance across areas.

questions.stem: Which is one of the intelligences in Gardner's original theory?
options: emotional quotient
fluid reasoning
general factor g
bodily-kinaesthetic
questions.explanation: Gardner's original seven intelligences were linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal and intrapersonal. Naturalist intelligence was added later.

questions.stem: A critic says Gardner's theory is appealing but weak as science. What is the critic's most likely reason?
options: Some intelligences are better seen as talents and are hard to measure
It reduces intelligence to a single score that is given by an IQ test
It was based only on the scores of one adopted child and her parents
It ignores the abilities that are valued outside of school settings
questions.explanation: Critics argue that abilities like musical or bodily skill are talents rather than intelligences, and that there are few valid tests of each intelligence. Gardner's theory deliberately rejects a single IQ score.

questions.stem: Sternberg's triarchic theory identifies which three kinds of intelligence?
options: general, specific and fluid
verbal, performance and full scale
analytical, creative and practical
linguistic, spatial and musical
questions.explanation: Sternberg proposed analytical (componential), creative (experiential) and practical (contextual) intelligence. Linguistic, spatial and musical are among Gardner's intelligences.

questions.stem: A farmer with little schooling repairs machinery with whatever parts are at hand and adapts quickly to changing weather and markets. In Sternberg's theory this mainly shows:
options: analytical intelligence
creative intelligence
the general factor, g
practical intelligence
questions.explanation: Practical (contextual) intelligence is the ability to adapt to, shape and select real-world environments, often called street smarts. Analytical intelligence is what school tests mainly measure.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares Spearman's and Sternberg's theories?
options: Both theories describe eight independent intelligences of roughly equal value
Spearman stressed one general ability; Sternberg added skills used in life
Spearman proposed three abilities; Sternberg proposed a single general ability
Both theories argue that intelligence is fully measured by standard IQ tests
questions.explanation: Spearman emphasised a single general factor measured well by IQ tests. Sternberg argued that tests capture mainly analytical ability and added creative and practical intelligence.

questions.stem: In Bouchard and McGue's (1981) review, identical twins reared together had a higher IQ correlation (about 0.86) than fraternal twins reared together (about 0.60). This suggests:
options: the environment has no influence on intelligence
fraternal twins share more genes than identical twins
identical twins are raised in different environments
genes contribute to differences in intelligence
questions.explanation: Both kinds of twins reared together share similar environments, but identical twins share all their genes, so their higher correlation points to a genetic contribution. It does not rule out environmental influence.

questions.stem: In Bouchard and McGue's review, identical twins reared apart still had a high IQ correlation (about 0.72), though lower than those reared together. What does the difference between the two suggest?
options: Genes have no effect on intelligence in separated twins
Separated twins have fewer genes in common with each other
Intelligence is entirely determined by the home environment
The shared environment also contributes to intelligence
questions.explanation: The high correlation for twins reared apart shows a strong genetic influence, while the drop compared with twins reared together shows that sharing an environment also matters. This supports an interactionist view.

questions.stem: Why might identical twins reared apart still have quite similar environments?
options: Researchers deliberately raise them in identical conditions to control variables
They are often placed in similar homes, and similar traits draw similar responses
They share fewer genes than fraternal twins, so their surroundings must be the same
They are always adopted by the same family members after being separated at birth
questions.explanation: Adoption agencies often place children in homes similar to their birth families, and twins' shared looks and temperament can draw similar treatment. This means genetic and environmental effects can be confounded.

questions.stem: In Scarr and Weinberg's Minnesota adoption studies, children adopted into advantaged homes scored above the average expected for their background. This shows that:
options: intelligence test scores can be raised by an enriched environment
intelligence is fixed at birth and cannot be changed by the home
adopted children share most of their genes with adoptive parents
IQ tests are unreliable when they are used with adopted children
questions.explanation: The adoptive homes raised the children's average scores, showing that intelligence is malleable and responsive to environment. Scarr and Weinberg also found that individual differences still related to biological parents.

questions.stem: In adoption studies, a closer IQ correlation between adopted children and their biological parents than their adoptive parents is evidence for:
options: cultural bias in the test that was used
the Flynn effect over several generations
a genetic influence on intelligence
an environmental influence on intelligence
questions.explanation: Biological parents share genes but not the home environment with the adopted child, so a closer correlation with them points to genetic influence. A closer match with adoptive parents would point to the environment.

questions.stem: The concept of reaction range proposes that:
options: a person's IQ score changes randomly each time an intelligence test is taken
genes set upper and lower limits, and environment decides where a person falls
intelligence is fixed at conception and the environment has no effect on it at all
intelligence increases by the same amount in every person as they grow older
questions.explanation: Reaction range describes a genetically set range of possible outcomes. An enriched environment allows development towards the top of the range and a deprived one towards the bottom.

questions.stem: Two children have the same genetic reaction range. One grows up in a deprived home, the other in an enriched home. According to the reaction range concept:
options: the enriched child can score well beyond the upper limit of the range
the enriched child is likely to score towards the top of the shared range
both children will score exactly the same because their genes are the same
the deprived child will score above the range because of extra effort
questions.explanation: With the same range, environment determines where each child falls. The enriched child is likely to reach nearer the upper limit and the deprived child nearer the lower limit; neither goes outside the range.

questions.stem: Turkheimer and colleagues (2003) studied twins from families of different socioeconomic status (SES). What did they find?
options: Socioeconomic status had no relationship with the IQ scores of the twins at all
In poorer families, environment explained most IQ differences; in richer ones, genes did
In poorer families, genes explained most IQ differences; in richer ones, environment did
Genes explained the same share of IQ differences at every level of family income
questions.explanation: Turkheimer found heritability of IQ was close to zero in low-SES families, where shared environment accounted for most variation, and much higher in high-SES families. Genetic potential shows more when the environment is good.

questions.stem: What does Turkheimer's finding suggest about heritability estimates for intelligence?
options: They depend on the environment of the population studied
They are fixed numbers that apply to every population
They measure how much of a person's own IQ comes from genes
They show that intelligence cannot be changed by schooling
questions.explanation: Heritability describes the share of differences within a particular population that relates to genes, and it changes with conditions. It cannot be applied to an individual or used to argue that intelligence is unchangeable.

questions.stem: Children raised in an institution with little stimulation and few interactions with caregivers later score lower on intelligence tests. This illustrates the effect of:
options: environmental enrichment
the Flynn effect
cultural bias
environmental deprivation
questions.explanation: A deprived environment lacks the stimulation, interaction and resources that support intellectual development. Studies show that early, prolonged deprivation is linked to lower later scores.

questions.stem: In animal studies, young rats kept with playthings and companions grew a thicker cortex than rats housed alone in empty cages. This supports the idea that:
options: a deprived environment improves learning ability
rats and humans develop in exactly the same way
an enriched environment promotes brain development
brain development is fixed by the genes at birth
questions.explanation: The enriched condition provided stimulation and social contact, and the rats' brains showed more growth. This supports the influence of enrichment, though generalising from rats to humans needs care.

questions.stem: The Flynn effect refers to:
options: the higher IQ correlation of identical than fraternal twins
the decline in IQ scores that is seen in very old age
the steady rise in average IQ scores across generations
the drop in IQ scores of children in deprived environments
questions.explanation: Flynn showed that average raw scores on IQ tests rose by about three points per decade during the 20th century in many countries, so tests had to be re-normed.

questions.stem: Why does the Flynn effect support an environmental influence on intelligence?
options: The rise is too fast to be explained by genetic change
The rise shows that intelligence is fully inherited from parents
The rise happened only in children who were raised by adoptive parents
The rise proves that IQ tests have become less reliable over time
questions.explanation: Gene pools change very slowly, so a large rise within a few generations points to environmental causes such as better nutrition, more schooling and more complex environments.

questions.stem: Which is a likely environmental explanation for the Flynn effect?
options: the use of the ratio formula for calculating IQ scores
a fall in the number of identical twins being born
better nutrition and longer, more widespread schooling
a rapid increase in the genes linked to intelligence
questions.explanation: Improved nutrition, health, education and exposure to abstract thinking are the main proposed explanations. Genetic change could not occur quickly enough.

questions.stem: A study finds a correlation of +0.45 between parents' and children's IQ scores. Why can this not be used alone to show that intelligence is inherited?
options: A correlation of +0.45 shows that no relationship exists
IQ scores of children cannot be compared with adults' scores
The correlation shows the parents' scores caused the children's
Parents and children share environments as well as genes
questions.explanation: Biological parents usually raise their children, so shared genes and shared environment are confounded. Twin and adoption studies are used to try to separate them.

questions.stem: A psychologist argues that neither nature nor nurture alone explains a person's IQ. This is the interactionist position, which holds that:
options: genes and environment combine to shape a person's intelligence
intelligence is shaped mainly by schooling and not by genes at all
intelligence is determined entirely by genes inherited from parents
intelligence is a single ability measured completely by IQ tests
questions.explanation: Interactionism holds that genetic potential and environmental influences work together. Reaction range and Turkheimer's findings both show how the environment affects how genetic potential is expressed.

questions.stem: Intellectual potential refers to:
options: the IQ score a person achieves on their first intelligence test
the average IQ score of all the people in a person's age group
the amount by which IQ scores rise from one generation to the next
the level of ability a person could reach in ideal conditions
questions.explanation: Intellectual potential is the highest level a person could reach given their genes and the best possible environment. Measured IQ reflects how far that potential has been developed.

questions.stem: A psychologist wants to study the effect of early deprivation on intelligence. Why can she not run a true experiment on this question?
options: Intelligence cannot be measured with any reliability in children
Deprivation is a dependent variable, so it cannot be manipulated
Experiments cannot be used in psychology to study development
It would be unethical to assign children to a deprived environment
questions.explanation: Deliberately depriving children would cause harm and could never be approved by an ethics committee. Researchers instead study children who have experienced deprivation, such as in some orphanages, which limits conclusions about cause.
